stem: Which region of the brain is responsible for moving your right hand?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Two independent facts must both be right:

  • Precentral gyrus (the ridge in front of the central sulcus) = primary motor cortex, part of the frontal lobe. The postcentral gyrus (behind the sulcus) = primary sensory cortex, receiving touch, proprioception, vibration, pain and temperature, part of the parietal lobe.
  • The left motor cortex controls the right side of the body, and vice versa.

stem: Which area of the brain is responsible for taste?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The insular cortex is responsible for taste.

  • Corpus callosum — connects the two hemispheres
  • Uncus — smell. The key's mnemonic: "you can smell your uncle, but you shouldn't taste him"
  • Cingulate gyrus — part of the limbic system (emotion and memory)
  • Broca's area — coordinates the motor movements involved in speech

stem: A large blood clot in the cavernous sinus compressed one of the nerves running through the lateral wall of the sinus resulting in numbness of the left upper eyelid, eyebrow, and forehead. Which nerve did it compress?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Two filters:

  1. What runs where — CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus; CN VI runs through the sinus; the optic nerve runs above it, carrying visual input from the retina to the LGN of the thalamus. That eliminates A and E.
  2. What is numb — CN III, IV and VI are motor to the eye, so they cannot cause numbness. V1 (ophthalmic) supplies the upper eyelid, eyebrow and forehead; V2 (maxillary) supplies the cheeks and maxillary teeth.

stem: A patient presents with unilateral facial paralysis and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Imaging reveals a mass in the posterior fossa of the brainstem. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected by the mass?
answer: The correct answer is C. The facial nerve (CN VII). The loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is due to the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve — pair that with the facial paralysis and CN VII accounts for both findings at once. Contrast Q77, where taste to the posterior third is the discriminator.

stem: Which of the following cranial nerves is correctly matched with one of its targets?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The trigeminal nerve handles sensory perception of the face and controls the muscles of mastication (via V3).

Every distractor is a real pairing with the wrong nerve attached:

  • Lateral rectus → abducens (VI); abducens abducts
  • Parotid gland → glossopharyngeal (IX) — C is the best trap in the question, because the facial nerve does travel through the parotid gland without innervating it
  • Sternocleidomastoid → spinal accessory (XI)
  • Intrinsic tongue muscles → hypoglossal (XII)

stem: Which of the following is consistent with a lesion of cranial nerve III?

options.html: Contralateral pupil is deviated superiorly and laterally
Ipsilateral pupil is deviated inferiorly and laterally

answer:
The correct answer is E. CN III (oculomotor) drives ipsilateral pupillary constriction and eyelid elevation, plus all ipsilateral extraocular muscles except lateral rectus and superior oblique — the mnemonic LR6, SO4.

So a CN III lesion gives: pupil dilation, ptosis, and deviation of the eye inferiorly (because the still-working superior oblique pulls it down) and laterally (because the still-working lateral rectus pulls it out) — the classic "down and out". All findings are ipsilateral, which kills B and D. C is CN VII, which closes the eye.

flags.title: Muscle slip in the key
flags.html: The key writes "superior rectus moves it inferiorly and slightly medially from the neutral position". It means superior oblique, which is the muscle spared by a CN III lesion and the reason the eye deviates down. Superior rectus is CN III-innervated and elevates the eye.

Motor innervation to muscles of face
Parasympathetic innervation to submandibular and sublingual glands

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to your clinic with acute facial paralysis. He is able to raise his forehead normally and has left facial weakness. He has a history of hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia and smoking. What is the most likely cause of his facial weakness?

options.html: Right-sided stroke affecting right motor cortex
Left-sided stroke affecting left motor cortex

answer:
The correct answer is A. The forehead receives innervation from both the left and right motor cortices, so a right-sided stroke gives left facial weakness with normal forehead raising — forehead sparing is the hallmark of an upper motor neuron lesion.

Bell's palsy (B) is the trap, because it is the common cause of acute facial paralysis — but Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion and would not spare the forehead (see Q125). Also note the stroke risk factors stacked in the stem: hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking.

stem: Which of the following presenting features is not a prognostic variable for Bell's palsy?

options.html: Late onset of return of facial function
All of the above are prognostic variables

answer:
The correct answer is E. All of them are prognostic. The good prognostic variables for Bell's palsy:

  • Incomplete palsy — 94% of patients progress to full recovery
  • Early onset of return of function — return within 1 week → ~90% recover; 2nd week → 83%; 3rd week → 60%
  • Age < 60 years
  • Normal hearing and tearing
  • No diabetes and no hypertension

Note B is phrased as the bad version ("late onset of return") — it is still a prognostic variable, just an adverse one, which is exactly why E is correct.

stem: A patient presents with left facial weakness with the left forehead being spared. These symptoms could be attributed to a:
answer:
The correct answer is D. The forehead is supplied by both motor cortices, so a right-sided stroke gives left facial weakness with the left forehead spared — the left forehead still has input from the left motor cortex.

The rule in one line: an UMN lesion is forehead-sparing; a LMN lesion affects the entire face, because the facial nerve itself is damaged and no signal gets through at all. Same principle as Q78, and the reason Bell's palsy involves the whole hemiface. See facial nerve palsy.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Cortical syndromes, language & apraxia
lectureMeta: Workbook Q5, Q8, Q34, Q36-Q37. Tests [[10 - Cortical Syndromes]].
stem: Susan speaks fluently and with normal intonation and grammar, but has difficulty communicating. She uses the wrong or nonsensical words, omits words, and makes up words, making it impossible to get a point across. What is Susan's diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Aphasias are due to damage to language areas or their connections, in the dominant hemisphere.

  • Wernicke's aphasia — a fluent aphasia; Wernicke's area handles comprehension of language and helps you come up with what you want to say, so a lesion gives fluent, nonsensical speech and writing.
  • Broca's aphasia — speech and writing are laboured and broken, because Broca's area produces the motor commands for the words (spoken, written or signed).
  • Dysarthria — a motor speech disorder giving poor articulation. Not a language problem.
  • Aphonia — inability to produce sounds.
  • Auditory agnosia — the auditory association cortex is damaged, so you cannot understand what you hear; you could still read and write.

options.html: Hypoglycemia in the setting of a structural lesion

answer: The correct answer is F — all of the above. All options may cause aphasia. The teaching point is that hypocalcemia belongs on the list too, which is what separates F from E — metabolic derangements can unmask focal deficits, so the differential is not purely structural.

stem: Which term describes someone who is unable to use a hair brush, despite having the strength to use it?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Apraxia is a cortical syndrome: inability to carry out a motor task despite having the power to complete it. The phrase "despite having the strength" in the stem is the definitional cue.

  • Ataxia — lack of coordination in movement
  • Aphasia — a language deficit (comprehension, production, or both)
  • Agnosia — inability to recognize objects, persons and sounds despite otherwise normal sensation

lecture: Localization: cortex, thalamus & brainstem
lectureMeta: Workbook Q22-Q25, Q30-Q31. Tests [[12 - Approach to Localization]], [[03 - Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon]].
stem: A 73-year-old male complains of a sudden onset of numbness and weakness of the right side of his body. His face, arm, and hand are more affected than his leg, foot, and genitals. He also developed a Wernicke's aphasia. A clot in which of the following arteries would best explain his symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is B. This is the section's model localization walk-through, in three steps.

1. Which side of the brain? Findings on the patient's right face and right arm plus language impairment localize to the left hemisphere — most people are left-hemisphere dominant for language (Broca's and Wernicke's areas).

2. Which level? Not brainstem — a brainstem lesion gives crossed findings (opposite sides of face and body). Not spinal cord — a right cord lesion could give right arm weakness and numbness, but language is cortical and would be preserved, as would facial movement and sensation, which are cranial-nerve mediated.

3. Which artery? You need two things — the homuncular organization and the vascular territories:

  • Lateral to medial, the pre- and post-central gyri run HAL: Head, Arm, Leg
  • ACA → medial frontal and parietal lobes (hence leg/foot/genitals)
  • MCA → lateral frontal, parietal and temporal lobes (hence face and arm more than leg)
  • PCA → medial and inferior temporal and occipital surfaces
  • Labyrinthine artery → inner ear; basilar artery → branches to cerebellum, pons, midbrain

Face and arm affected more than leg, plus aphasia, on the right body = left MCA.

stem: A 38-year-old female presents with vertigo, facial numbness, diplopia, and dysphagia. An MRI shows a mass in the pons region. Which of the following cranial nerves is most likely affected by the mass?
answer: The correct answer is B. The pons contains CN V, VI, VII and VIII — so the question is which of those best explains the cluster. Facial numbness points to the trigeminal nerve (CN V), which carries sensation from the face and also controls the muscles of chewing.

flags.title: The key hedges, and one symptom does not fit
flags.html: The key concedes that diplopia suggests CN VI and then adds that "because the mass is in the pons region, it is most likely affecting multiple cranial nerves" — which does not actually justify picking a single letter. Dysphagia is worse: it is a CN IX/X (medullary) function, not a pontine one at all. Take B as the best-of-a-flawed-set answer; the durable content is the pons = V, VI, VII, VIII grouping.

stem: A patient recently developed drooping of the lower half of their face on the left-hand side, as well as right hemiparesis (weakness of the right side of their body). Their left eye is noticeably drier and their left pupil is now deviated medially. Sounds seem louder in their left ear. What is the most likely location of the lesion?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Three steps.

1. Crossed findings = brainstem. Weakness of the left face and right body is the signature: cranial nerves innervate the ipsilateral face, while corticospinal neurons in the brainstem innervate the contralateral body. So the lesion is on the left side of the brainstem.

2. Which cranial nerves? → which level. The nerves involved are CN VI and CN VII, and the pons is where both exit the brainstem.

3. Check every finding against those two nerves:

  • CN VI lesion → medial deviation of the eye, because lateral rectus no longer abducts it
  • CN VII normally supplies muscles of facial expression, stapedius (which dampens noise), taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue, and the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands — so a CN VII lesion gives lower-face paralysis, hyperacusis (sounds louder), impaired taste, and dry mouth and dry eyes. That accounts for the droop, the loud ear and the dry eye.

stem: A patient is experiencing dysarthria in addition to hemiplegia and loss of touch and proprioception on the right side of his body. What is the most likely location of the lesion?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The reasoning narrows in stages:

1. Side and possible levels. Right-body weakness could come from the left brain (motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem) or the right spinal cord, peripheral nerve, NMJ or muscle.

2. Why a "convergence zone". Because a large part of the body (both arm and leg) is affected and there are both motor and sensory findings, the lesion must be somewhere sensory and motor fibres for an entire side lie close together — internal capsule/thalamus, brainstem, or spinal cord.

3. The dysarthria localizes it. Dysarthria (slurred speech) comes from impairment of the hypoglossal nerve or its nucleus in the medulla — poor tongue control impairs speech. (It could also come from a CN X palsy, which also arises from the medulla.) So: left medulla.

4. Where within the medulla. Anteriorly, because the pyramids are involved; and medially, because touch and proprioception rather than pain and temperature are impaired — the medial lemniscus is more medial than the spinothalamic tract. And the reason there are no crossed sensory findings (no left-face sensory loss) is that the CN V nucleus sits more laterally.

On option A: a lesion in the LEFT VPL could cause loss of all sensory modalities on the right body, and if large enough could extend into the internal capsule to add hemiparesis — but even then it would not be the best answer, because it does not account for the dysarthria. (And the option as printed says Right VPL, which is the wrong side entirely.)

stem: When you put a prism in front of your eye before throwing darts, the dartboard appears displaced to one side and you miss. After repetition, you eventually adjust for the prism and start throwing more accurately. Which region of the brain is most important in helping you learn how to hit your target?
answer: The correct answer is B. The cerebellum and hippocampus are both involved in learning, but they learn different things: the cerebellum learns motor movements, the hippocampus learns facts (declarative memory). Prism adaptation is motor recalibration, so it is cerebellar.

lecture: Tone, reflexes & the approach to weakness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35, Q38, Q48-Q49, Q54, Q65, Q85. Tests [[07 - Neurophysiology of Reflexes]], [[11 - Approach to Weakness]].
stem: All of the following are consistent with an upper motor neuron pattern of weakness except:
answer:
The correct answer is C. Damage to an upper motor neuron (a corticospinal neuron) initially causes loss of muscle tone, but with time the patient develops spasticity, because of increased motor neuron sensitivity to the remaining inputs — hence spastic hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and clonus on rapid dorsiflexion.

The Babinski sign (upgoing toe) is also seen in infants, because the corticospinal tract is not yet fully developed — a useful sanity check on what the sign means.

On C: UMN weakness can produce some atrophy from disuse, but it is not as significant as the atrophy of lower motor neuron weakness — which is the discriminator being tested.

lecture: Tone, reflexes & the approach to weakness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35, Q38, Q48-Q49, Q54, Q65, Q85. Tests [[07 - Neurophysiology of Reflexes]], [[11 - Approach to Weakness]].
stem: You suspect a patient has experienced nerve root damage and you want to quickly determine the extent of the injury (ie find out which nerve roots are affected), which of the following tests would be most helpful for localizing the lesion?

options.html: Use a cotton swab on different parts of their body to test light touch
Test the sensation in various dermatomes using pinprick
See if they can tell when a tuning fork is vibrating and when it is not
Ask the patient to tell you whether you're moving their fingers up or down
Perform a detailed cranial nerve exam

answer: The correct answer is B. Each spinal nerve's territory overlaps slightly with that of the adjacent nerve, blurring the edges of the dermatome — and crucially the overlap is greater for touch than for pain. That makes pinprick (pain) a more precise test for segmental nerve injury than light touch.

stem: A 53-year-old man has a several month history of weakness affecting his limbs, eye lids, and speech. He notices that his ptosis worsens throughout the day, his speech gets slurred if he talks for extended periods of time and it becomes more difficult for him to use his arms — for example to wash his hair — later in the day. Where would you localize his problem to?
answer: The correct answer is E. The fluctuating course of the weakness makes neuromuscular junction pathology most likely — myasthenia gravis or Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. These conditions cause weakness with continuing activity that improves with rest, and commonly affect both limb and cranial-nerve-innervated muscles, which is why his eyelids, speech and arms are all involved.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q35, Q38, Q48-Q49, Q54, Q65, Q85. Tests [[07 - Neurophysiology of Reflexes]], [[11 - Approach to Weakness]].
stem: A 64-year-old woman complains of difficulty standing up from a chair or walking up stairs. She says she has to push off of the armrests or pull herself up using the banister while performing these tasks. She has no difficulty doing up buttons or tying her shoes. She has no sensory deficits. What is the most likely site of localization?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Proximal muscle weakness plus no sensory deficits points to a myopathy.

The proximal/distal split is the localizing tool:

  • Proximal weakness — difficulty standing from a chair, or getting arms above the head (changing a lightbulb, washing hair) → myopathy, e.g. polymyositis, dermatomyositis, muscular dystrophy
  • Distal weakness — difficulty tying shoes, doing up buttons, writing → peripheral neuropathy

lecture: Tone, reflexes & the approach to weakness
lectureMeta: Workbook Q35, Q38, Q48-Q49, Q54, Q65, Q85. Tests [[07 - Neurophysiology of Reflexes]], [[11 - Approach to Weakness]].
stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a tingling sensation in his toes and progressive weakness in both legs. He has bloody diarrhea, nausea and vomiting and cramps 3 weeks ago that lasted for a few days. He has not traveled recently and had not eaten anything unusual. Physical examination reveals markedly decreased patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy – Guillain Barré Syndrome (GBS)

answer:
The correct answer is B. GBS findings: rapidly progressive, symmetric, ascending flaccid paralysis involving legs, arms and often the face; cranial nerve deficits giving dysphagia, dysarthria and facial weakness; papilledema; autonomic dysfunction; and respiratory muscle paralysis in extreme cases.

The preceding illness is the diagnostic clue: 2/3 of patients have an antecedent event such as URTI or GI illness. Most commonly implicated: viral (CMV, EBV, HIV, hepatitis) or bacterial (Campylobacter jejuni, mycoplasma) — and bloody diarrhea 3 weeks ago is textbook Campylobacter.

Investigations: NCS showing demyelination; CSF showing elevated protein with normal cell count. Treatment: supportive care plus either plasma exchange or IVIg. Monitor pulmonary function with peak flow studies to assess for respiratory failure.

stem: A patient presents complaining of new onset motor weakness in the legs. On exam you find normal light touch and vibration sensation in the legs but a loss of pain and temperature sensation. What is this condition called?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Anterior cord syndrome usually arises from a clot in the anterior spinal artery — the only blood supply to the anterior cord. The posterior cord is still supplied by the 2 posterior spinal arteries, so the DCML running up the posterior cord is spared — which is why touch and vibration are normal.

The anatomy predicts the deficits exactly: the anterior cord contains the ventral horns (motor) and, more laterally, the lateral spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature). Compare Q44, the same syndrome asked from the etiology side.

lecture: Somatosensation & the pain pathways
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39-Q40, Q51. Tests [[05 - Neurophysiology of Sensation]].
stem: Why is your 2-point discrimination worse on your back than it is on your finger?

options.html: The skin on your back has a higher density of receptors
Afferents are more closely spaced on your back than on your finger
The skin on your back has a very high tactile acuity
Each dorsal column neuron from your back has a small receptive field
In the back, many afferents converge onto a single dorsal column neuron

answer: The correct answer is E. The back has lower tactile acuity and its dorsal column neurons have larger receptive fields, because it has a lower density of receptors and a greater number of afferents converge onto a single dorsal column neuron. Every other option states one half of that picture backwards.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Somatosensation & the pain pathways
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39-Q40, Q51. Tests [[05 - Neurophysiology of Sensation]].
stem: Which of the following pain management techniques would specifically target the spinothalamic pathway?

options.html: Transection of anterior commissure in the spinal cord
Stimulation of the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus
Administration of NSAID medication, such as advil
Administration of a tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline

answer:
The correct answer is A. Spinothalamic fibres cross the midline at the level they enter the spinal cord, via the anterior commissure, before ascending contralaterally — so transecting the anterior commissure hits that pathway and nothing else.

Note the word specifically in the stem — every other option works, just not selectively:

  • VPL (B) also carries dorsal column information
  • NSAIDs (C) act peripherally, blocking prostaglandin production
  • Motor cortex stimulation (D) has an unclear mechanism and is not specific
  • TCAs (E) block reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin in the dorsal horn — key components of the descending inhibitory pathway (see Q51) — but act in many places throughout the body

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Somatosensation & the pain pathways
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39-Q40, Q51. Tests [[05 - Neurophysiology of Sensation]].
stem: Fill in the blank with one correct answer within the bracket beside it. The __________ (dorsal, ventral) horn of the spinal cord serves as an interface in pain processing. __________ (serotonin, dopamine, NE, GABA) and __________ (serotonin, dopamine, NE, GABA) are key neurotransmitters in descending inhibitory pain pathways. __________ (increased, decreased) availability may promote pain inhibition centrally.
answer:
dorsal; serotonin, NE; increased.

The dorsal horn is the interface for pain processing; serotonin and norepinephrine are the key descending-inhibitory neurotransmitters; and increased availability promotes central pain inhibition. This is exactly why TCAs work for neuropathic pain — see Q40E, where amitriptyline blocks reuptake of both.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A 37-year-old man was in a motor vehicle collision. After the accident, he had numbness from his chest down, as well as on the medial side of his arms, forearms, and hands. He lost the ability to feel pain and temperature as well as touch, vibration, and proprioception in those areas. Sensation was preserved on his head, neck, lateral aspect of arms, forearms and hands, and on his thumbs. He also had flaccid paralysis of all muscles in his legs as well as his triceps, wrist flexors, finger extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles. His deltoid, bicep and brachioradialis strength was preserved bilaterally. He has lost control of bowel and bladder. Where is the lesion?

options.html: Bilateral VPL and internal capsule lesions
Anterior spinal cord lesion at C5-C6 level
Complete spinal cord lesion at C6-C7 level

answer:
The correct answer is D. Three separate determinations:

1. Level. The cord is affected at and below C7, which exits between the C6 and C7 vertebrae. Remember there are 8 cervical nerve roots but 7 cervical vertebrae, so the first 7 roots exit above their corresponding vertebra while C8 exits below C7. C6 is the last intact root — hence normal thumb sensation and normal biceps and brachioradialis strength.

2. Complete, not anterior. Because all sensory modalities are affected, this is a complete cord lesion. Anterior cord lesions spare the dorsal columns, leaving touch, vibration and proprioception intact (see Q44, Q65).

3. Why not the others. A — a bilateral VPL + internal capsule lesion could cause bilateral sensory and motor deficits, but a single cord lesion is far more likely than multiple brain lesions. B — a C7-8 root injury would not explain the lower limb findings. E — lumbar plexus involvement would not explain the upper limb findings.

And note the flaccid paralysis: upper motor neuron damage causes initial flaccid paralysis before hypertonicity and spasticity develop — so flaccidity here does not argue for a lower motor neuron lesion (compare Q35).

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A patient is experiencing left leg weakness, and loss of light touch, vibration, and proprioception in the left leg along with loss of pain and temperature sensation in the right leg. Localize the lesion:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Hemitransection of the cord = Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral weakness and loss of light touch/proprioception/vibration, contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

The decussation levels explain the split: dorsal column fibres travel ipsilaterally until the medulla, whereas spinothalamic fibres cross at the level of the spinal cord before ascending. So the side with the dorsal column loss is the side of the lesion — left.

Level: a cervical lesion would likely affect the upper limbs too, not just the lower. A thoracic lesion blocks traffic between the lumbosacral cord and the brain, affecting the lower extremities only.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A patient is referred to your neurology clinic for their B12 deficiency. On examination, you find a loss of light touch, proprioception and vibration up to the umbilicus, with preserved pinprick and temperature sensation. No motor weakness is noted. Where is the lesion?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A posterior cord lesion affects the dorsal column, giving loss of light touch, proprioception and vibration at and below that level with pain and temperature spared.

The level comes from the landmark: T10 nerve roots supply sensation to the umbilicus.

And the etiology fits: posterior cord syndromes occur as a consequence of B12 deficiency or syphilis — which is why the stem opens with the B12 deficiency.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A 72-year-old woman suddenly experiences motor weakness and loss of pain and temperature sensation in her legs with preserved light touch, vibration and proprioception. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?

options.html: Embolisms in her anterior spinal artery
An infectious process, such as Syphilis
Atherosclerosis of her posterior spinal artery

answer:
The correct answer is A. Bilateral loss of pain, temperature and motor function with sparing of the dorsal column is an anterior cord syndrome, which can be caused by disruption of the anterior spinal artery supplying that territory.

This is the exact mirror of Q43: B12 deficiency and syphilis more commonly cause a posterior cord syndrome — so B, D and E all point the wrong way, and C would affect all modalities (Q41).

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: Which of the following is MOST consistent with a central cord syndrome?

options.html: More weakness in the lower extremities compared to the upper ones
Loss of light touch, vibration and proprioception above the level of the injury
Contralateral weakness and ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
Lower motor neuron pattern of weakness below the level of the lesion
Bilateral loss of pain and temperature at the affected level

answer:
The correct answer is E. The bilateral loss of pain and temperature at the affected level is due to disruption of the pain and temperature fibres crossing the midline via the anterior commissure — the fibres that Q40 asks about surgically.

The full picture of central cord syndrome, which corrects each distractor:

  • Upper motor neuron pattern of weakness below the lesion, from corticospinal tract disruption — so D has the neuron type wrong
  • The patient may also get lower motor neuron weakness at the level, if the anterior horn cell is affected
  • The upper extremities are usually more affected than the lower — so A is backwards. The reason: corticospinal neurons innervating cervical regions run more medially than those going to lumbar regions, so a central lesion hits the cervical fibres first
  • Sensory loss below the lesion varies with the degree of dorsal column and spinothalamic involvement — so B has the direction wrong
  • C is Brown-Sequard syndrome (Q42)

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A 54-year-old presents with back pain that radiates down the lateral aspect of the leg into the foot. On examination, strength is reduced in foot dorsiflexion, toe extension, foot inversion, and foot eversion. On physical exam, you note that he has decreased sensation to the lateral aspect of the lower leg and dorsum of the foot. He has down-going toes and no spasticity is noted. Localize the lesion.
answer:
The correct answer is D. Two determinations:

  • Lower motor neuron, not upper: the atrophied muscle, hyporeflexive joint, down-going toes and lack of spasticity all point to an LMN lesion — i.e. a radiculopathy, not a cord syndrome.
  • Level: localized to L5 by the L5 dermatome — lateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot — and by the myotome (dorsiflexion, toe extension, inversion and eversion).

lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: A 61-year-old female sees her family doctor for shooting pain in her neck that radiates down her right arm into her middle finger. On examination, you note that her right triceps and wrist flexors are atrophied and weak, and she has sensory deficits on her right middle finger. Her right triceps reflex is hyporeflexive. A disc herniation in which location would best explain her symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is D. A C6-7 posterolateral disc herniation compresses the C7 nerve root, giving lower motor neuron weakness of triceps and wrist flexors plus sensory deficits on the middle finger — all three of her findings.

The posterior-vs-posterolateral distinction is the other half of the question: posterior (central) herniations compress the spinal cord behind the disc, producing upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion — which is not what she has.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem:
Match the nerve injury terms (letters) to the definitions (numbers).

1) Functional block and demyelination; preservation of axon integrity (compression, transient ischemia); good prognosis with complete recovery with remyelination (2-3 months). 2) Transection of axons and connective tissue elements with complete loss of function distal to site of injury; regeneration may be limited by scarring; surgical exploration and repair are often warranted. 3) Wallerian degeneration with preservation of Schwann cells and basal lamina of endoneurium (many crush injuries); recovery may take place over many months (3-12 months) and may be incomplete, in particular if regeneration must take place over long distances.
answer:
1-A, 2-C, 3-B.

GradePathologyRecovery
Neurapraxiafunctional block and demyelination; axon intact (compression, transient ischemia)complete, with remyelination, 2-3 months
AxonotmesisWallerian degeneration but Schwann cells and basal lamina preserved (crush injuries)3-12 months, may be incomplete over long distances
Neuronotmesistransection of axons and connective tissue; complete loss of function distallylimited by scarring; often needs surgical repair

The escalating theme is how much scaffolding survives — that is what sets the ceiling on recovery.

lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: Jeff presents to the ER complaining of unsteadiness. Examination shows decreased sense of position, vibration, and stereognosis in all extremities. Jeff is unable to stand without wavering for more than a few seconds when his eyes are closed. There are no other abnormal findings. Jeff's lesion(s) is most likely in the:

options.html: Lateral columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally
Dorsal columns of the spinal cord, bilaterally

answer:
The correct answer is E. The dorsal columns convey well-localized fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and proprioception from skin and joints — and every one of Jeff's deficits (position sense, vibration, stereognosis) is on that list.

The eyes-closed detail is the clincher: losing balance only when vision is removed is a positive Romberg, which is proprioceptive rather than cerebellar.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: The spinal cord, cord syndromes & radiculopathy
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41-Q47, Q52-Q53, Q55. Tests [[08 - Spinal Cord]].
stem: The difference between radiculopathy and myelopathy is:

options.html: radiculopathy is dysfunction of a nerve root; myelopathy is dysfunction in the spinal cord
myelopathy is dysfunction in a nerve root; radiculopathy is dysfunction in the spinal cord
radiculopathies are more painful than myelopathies
myelopathies are typically caused by infection; radiculopathies are more often caused by metastases

answer: The correct answer is A. Radiculopathy = dysfunction of a nerve root (e.g. C4 radiculopathy). Myelopathy = functional disturbance or pathological change in the spinal cord. This is the distinction Q47 turns on clinically.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: If a person has an eyeball that is too long or a lens that is too round, what is their diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Myopia (near-sightedness) means you can only focus on close targets. The reason from the geometry: when objects are close they are larger, and their image can make it all the way to the back of a long eyeball; when far away they are too small to reach the retina of a long eye.

The four distractors are two matched pairs — eye vs. ear:

  • Hyperopia — far-sightedness; only distant objects focus
  • Presbyopia — age-related, a stiff lens that cannot adjust to close objects
  • Presbycusis — age-related hearing loss of high-pitched frequencies
  • Hyperacusis — over-sensitivity to certain noises

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: If a person has an eyeball that is too short or a lens that is too flat, what kind of lenses do they need in their glasses?
answer: The correct answer is A. Convex = convergent lenses help focus the light sooner, which is what a far-sighted person needs to see objects close to themselves. Concave = divergent lenses are for the near-sighted. Note that B and D name the same lens, as do A and "convergent".

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Which of the following is true regarding rods?

options.html: They have higher visual acuity than cones
They are responsible for colour vision
They are found primarily in the fovea
They are more sensitive to light than cones
Their function is tested using a Snellen eye chart

answer:
The correct answer is D. Rods are more sensitive to light than cones, hence "night vision". Every other option is a cone property:

  • Cones have higher visual acuity, are responsible for colour vision, and are what the Snellen chart tests.
  • The fovea contains primarily cones; the peripheral retina contains primarily rods.

lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: If a patient cannot see objects in the bottom right side of their vision (from both eyes), what type of visual deficit would this be called?
answer: The correct answer is C — right homonymous inferior quadrantanopia. Build the name from the three descriptors in the stem: right side of vision, both eyes (= homonymous), and only the bottom quarter (= inferior quadrantanopia rather than a full hemianopia). See homonymous hemianopia.

stem: How would vision be affected if a pituitary tumor compressed the optic chiasm?

options.html: Loss of left visual field bilaterally
Loss of right visual field bilaterally
Loss of vision in left eye

answer:
The correct answer is D. Fibres from the nasal half of each retina — which see objects in the temporal visual fields — are the ones that cross at the optic chiasm. Disrupting them therefore produces bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of temporal vision bilaterally).

The nasal-retina/temporal-field inversion is the whole trick, and is why E is the trap.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Damage to the inferior temporal lobe is more likely to cause which of the following visual deficits?
answer:
The correct answer is D. This requires the dorsal and ventral streams of vision:

StreamRouteFunction
Dorsal — the "where" pathwayoccipital → posterior parietal cortexspatial location, and selecting an appropriate action
Ventral — the "what" pathwayoccipital → inferior temporal lobeperception and recognition of objects

Because the lesion is in the inferior temporal lobe, the ventral system is damaged, so both perception (A) and recognition (C) of objects are affected — but spatial location (B) is spared. Hence D, not E.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Narrowing of which of the following could result in reduced vision in the left eye (from compression of the optic nerve)?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The left optic nerve carries visual input from the retina to the LGN of the thalamus and travels through the optic canal.

The foramen roster, which this question and Q19 between them cover:

  • Superior orbital fissure — CN III, IV, V1, VI
  • Supraorbital foramen — a branch of V1 continues through it
  • Foramen rotundum — V2
  • Foramen ovale — V3

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[01 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[02 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: A 15-year-old patient is unable to read a book unless it is held at arm's length. His eyeballs are too __________ so you prescribe him __________ lenses as he has __________.
answer:
The correct answer is B. He can only see things far away, so he is far-sighted (hyperopia), which means the eyeball is too short and the rays converge beyond the retina. A converging lens makes the rays converge sooner, landing them on the retina.

E is excluded by age: presbyopia is the age-related stiff-lens problem (Q6), not a 15-year-old's. Same physics as Q7.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Neuro-ophthalmology: eye movements & the pupil
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90-Q93, Q111. Tests [[09 - Neurophthalmology]], [[14 - Autonomic Nervous System]].
stem: A 50-year-old man comes to your clinic because he is seeing double. You determine he has a left abducens palsy. Which direction(s) is he incapable of moving his eye?
answer: The correct answer is C. The abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye (lateral gaze). Damage to the left abducens causes ipsilateral weakness of the left lateral rectus — so he cannot abduct the left eye. The name carries the function: abducens abducts.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Neuro-ophthalmology: eye movements & the pupil
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90-Q93, Q111. Tests [[09 - Neurophthalmology]], [[14 - Autonomic Nervous System]].
stem: You are evaluating a patient on their extraocular eye movements and want to test the action of superior rectus alone. Which of the directions do you tell the patient to look?

options.html: Left eye - abduct and up; Right eye - abduct and up
Left eye - adduct and up; Right eye - adduct and up
Left eye - abduct and down; Right eye - abduct and down
Left eye - adduct and down; Right eye - adduct and down

answer:
The correct answer is A. To test a muscle you test its primary action. In isolation the superior rectus elevates and adducts, with elevation primary — but the inferior oblique also elevates the eye, so its upward pull has to be eliminated.

The trick is the axis of the globe:

  • ABduct (toward the ear) → aligns the superior and inferior recti with the axis of the globe, so only they can move the eye up or down
  • ADduct (toward the nose) → aligns the superior/inferior obliques with the axis, making them the primary vertical movers

So abduct + elevate isolates superior rectus.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Neuro-ophthalmology: eye movements & the pupil
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90-Q93, Q111. Tests [[09 - Neurophthalmology]], [[14 - Autonomic Nervous System]].
stem: You are evaluating a patient in your family medicine practice who presents with an eye that is "up and in". Which nerve and muscle(s) are affected?

options.html: Oculomotor - medial rectus, inferior rectus, superior rectus, inferior oblique

answer:
The correct answer is B. CN IV (trochlear) innervates superior oblique, which normally depresses and abducts the eye ("down and out"). Lose it and the eye rests "up and in" — the exact opposite.

Note the mechanism of injury: the trochlear nerve is commonly injured by trauma because it is a thin nerve. And contrast Q29, where a CN III lesion leaves the eye "down and out" — the two palsies are mirror images.

stem: You are evaluating a patient with the classic symptoms of Horner Syndrome. Which of the following would you expect to see in this patient?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Horner's syndrome classically gives miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis — all ipsilateral — from a lesion of the cervical sympathetic trunk. So A (mydriasis), B (vasoconstriction) and C (diaphoresis) are each the opposite of what a sympathetic lesion produces.

Of the four, only the corneal reflex remains intact, because the long ciliary nerve (a branch of the optic nerve) carries the afferent limb of the corneal reflex, and only the sympathetic fibres travelling through it are lost. Those sympathetic fibres innervate the dilator pupillae, so losing them leaves the pupil CONSTRICTED.

Clinically useful corollary: the presence or absence of a corneal reflex distinguishes true Horner syndrome from a problem with the long ciliary nerve itself.

lecture: Neuro-ophthalmology: eye movements & the pupil
lectureMeta: Workbook Q90-Q93, Q111. Tests [[09 - Neurophthalmology]], [[14 - Autonomic Nervous System]].
stem: When you are using your eyes to track a plane flying across the sky in the distance, the type of eye movement you are using is:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Smooth pursuit allows tracking of objects moving across the field of vision without moving the head.

Two constraints that define it against the distractors: you cannot use smooth pursuit without a moving object, and pursuit differs from the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which only occurs when you turn your head while staring at a stationary object.

weekLabel: Week 13 - Localization, the Spinal Cord, Vision & Neuroradiology
lecture: Neuroradiology
lectureMeta: Workbook Q27, Q131. Tests [[15 - Neuroradiology]].
stem: Which of the following is true regarding CT scans?

options.html: CT scans are better than MRI's for looking at brain parenchyma
CT scans are rarely used to look for cranial bleeds
CT scans are better than MRI's at imaging the posterior fossa
Acute bleeds have high attenuation (are bright) on CT
Grey matter is darker than white matter on CT

answer:
The correct answer is D. The denser the material, the brighter it is on CT. Blood is much denser than water because it contains dense globin molecules — so acute bleeds are bright.

And the corollary worth knowing: as blood ages and the globin degrades, it loses its bright white appearance, becoming isodense and eventually hypodense relative to the brain. That is the basis for dating a bleed.

C is false for an anatomical reason: the posterior fossa is difficult to see clearly on CT because the petrous bone is very thick.

stem: A 26-year-old man had a bottle smashed on his pterion at a bar. He looked alert in the emergency room, but his friends said he was "pretty out of it" for a little while after he was hit. A CT scan showed a region of high-attenuation (brightness) that is biconvex (football-shaped). What is his most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. A fractured pterion can lacerate the middle meningeal artery, producing an epidural hematoma in which blood accumulates between the dural membrane and the skull.

Both distinguishing features follow from one fact — the dura is tightly adhered to the suture lines:

  • the collection is contained, giving the biconvex "football" shape (contrast Q18's crescent)
  • the containment is also why many patients have a lucid period after a brief loss of consciousness, before deteriorating into coma — exactly this patient's history

lecture: Head injury & intracranial hemorrhage
lectureMeta: Workbook Q15-Q18, Q82-Q83. Tests [[01 - Approach to Head Injuries]], [[10 - Neurosurgical Emergencies]].
stem: A 52-year-old patient experiences a sudden-onset of the "worst headache of their life". They have a stiff neck, nausea, and vomiting, and have a reduced level of consciousness. They have 25 pack-years of smoking, their blood pressure is 145/92, and their mother had a cerebral aneurysm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. A subarachnoid hemorrhage — for example from rupture of a berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis — puts blood in the CSF, which irritates the meninges and produces neck stiffness. (The other classic cause of meningeal-irritation neck stiffness is meningitis.) The rapid rise in intracranial pressure causes the horrible headache, nausea, vomiting and reduced level of consciousness.

Smoking, hypertension and a family history of cerebral aneurysms are all risk factors — the stem gives all three. Note that option A is the epidural hematoma of Q15 under its arterial name.

lecture: Head injury & intracranial hemorrhage
lectureMeta: Workbook Q15-Q18, Q82-Q83. Tests [[01 - Approach to Head Injuries]], [[10 - Neurosurgical Emergencies]].
stem: A patient with a suspected acute subarachnoid hemorrhage had no abnormalities noted on CT. Which investigation would you do next to determine if there is a bleed?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The subarachnoid space contains cerebrospinal fluid, so blood in the CSF — found by lumbar puncture — is suggestive of a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Why the blood tests fail: hematocrit (part of a CBC) would drop after large blood loss, but it is nonspecific and takes time — it only falls once fluid is reabsorbed and the red cells are diluted. D-dimer is a very nonspecific marker of clot formation. See also Q83.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lecture: Head injury & intracranial hemorrhage

stem: Sudden acceleration-deceleration of brain parenchyma can result in tearing of bridging veins. This injury is seen as a crescent-shaped hyperintensity on CT that may cross suture lines. What is the name of this type of injury?
answer:
The correct answer is A. When bridging veins rupture they bleed into the subdural space — which is a potential, not physiologic, space, since the arachnoid and dural membranes normally adhere to one another.

Two contrasts with Q15's epidural hematoma: acute bleeds are bright (hyperintense) on CT in both, but the blood in a subdural hematoma can cross suture lines, which an epidural cannot — hence crescent vs. biconvex.

stem: A 60-year-old woman arrives in the emergency department with a sudden severe headache ("thunderclap" headache) for the past couple of days. She has been experiencing nausea, vomiting and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The characteristic feature of subarachnoid hemorrhage is the sudden severe headache — "worst headache of my life" or "thunderclap". The patient may or may not also have a brief loss of consciousness, nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness and, rarely, focal deficits. Same presentation as Q16.

stem: A patient arrives in your clinic and after obtaining a history and physical examination, you suspect a subarachnoid hemorrhage. What are your next steps?

options.html: Administer prednisone as soon as possible
CT head and if there are no abnormal findings, perform a lumbar puncture
Immediately perform a lumbar puncture to find evidence of hemorrhage

answer:
The correct answer is C. The diagnosis of SAH cannot be made on clinical grounds alone. Imaging must confirm bleeding, and CT without contrast is the modality of choice — high sensitivity, correctly identifying over 95% of cases. If the CT is negative but suspicion remains high, then LP must be done to rule out occult blood.

E is wrong on sequencing, not on principle: the LP is right (Q17), but CT comes first.

stem: A 61-year-old overweight male has Type II diabetes and is a lifelong smoker. He also has high blood pressure and high cholesterol. The best way to reduce his risk of stroke is:
answer: The correct answer is D. Of the modifiable risk factors for stroke, lowering blood pressure is the best way to prevent it. All five options are genuine modifiable risk factors — the question is purely about which has the largest effect.

stem:
Questions 128, 129, and 130 are based on the following scenario: A 70-year-old RHD male develops acute onset left arm weakness and numbness. Within 24hrs he then goes on to start speaking nonsense that no one appears to understand. In the hospital you note that he has only shaved the right side of his face and has not put his arm through his left sleeve. On neurological examination he is unable to repeat phrases and follow three step commands however his fluency is unaffected. You are unable to check his strength and sensation as he cannot understand instructions but he is found to be hyperreflexic in his left arm.

Where does the language deficit localize to?
answer: The correct answer is B. Fluent aphasia localizes to Wernicke's area, in the dominant hemisphere. The stem gives the two halves of that: speaking nonsense with fluency unaffected, plus impaired comprehension (cannot follow three-step commands). Same logic as Q5.

stem: Where does the left arm weakness localize to?
answer: The correct answer is D. UMN signs are present in the left arm — the hyperreflexia — which localizes to the contralateral hemisphere, i.e. the right precentral gyrus (see Q3).

stem: What is the top differential diagnosis you must consider in a patient with acute multifocal stepwise cerebral lesions?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The number one diagnosis that must be ruled out is cardioembolic stroke — showers of emboli produce exactly this multifocal, stepwise pattern.

D is the near-miss: cerebral tumours can also have multifocal cerebral localizations, but the timeline is more subacute and slowly progressive (compare Q80).

lecture: Stroke: localization, investigation & prevention
lectureMeta: Workbook Q50, Q84, Q102, Q114, Q128-Q130, Q134, Q138. Tests [[03 - Approach to Stroke]].
stem: A 65-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the clinic following a recent ischemic stroke. Which of the following interventions would be considered appropriate for secondary prevention of future strokes?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Antiplatelet therapy such as daily low-dose aspirin is the cornerstone of secondary prevention after ischemic stroke.

The other three are all real interventions with narrower indications:

  • Anticoagulation — considered in specific cases such as atrial fibrillation, not routine secondary prevention
  • carotid endarterectomy — for selected patients with high-grade ICA stenosis
  • Weight loss — part of lifestyle modification to reduce risk factors, but not a primary intervention for secondary prevention

stem: Where is the lesion likely located in this patient with a stroke presenting with left-sided hemiparesis affecting the arm, leg, and upper lip, but no sensory deficits?

flags.title: This question is broken — do not learn a letter from it
flags.html:
The key prints D (left insula) and justifies it with a false premise: "The left insula is a region of the brain responsible for motor control of the left side of the body."

Two errors in one sentence. First, the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body (this section's own Q3, Q22, Q125 and Q129 all say so) — so left-sided hemiparesis requires a right-sided lesion, and every option is labelled "Left". Second, the insula is not primary motor cortex and is not the structure responsible for motor control.

What the question was probably reaching for: a purely motor hemiparesis affecting arm, leg and face together with no sensory loss is the classic pure motor lacune of the internal capsule — the motor fibres are packed tightly there while the sensory fibres run separately, so a small lesion can spare sensation entirely. A cortical lesion large enough to hit arm, leg and face would almost certainly involve the adjacent sensory strip. So the intended answer is most likely "internal capsule", on the right. Treat this item as a reasoning exercise, not a fact.

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lecture: Multiple sclerosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q1. Tests [[02 - Multiple Sclerosis]].
stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic of multiple sclerosis?

options.html: It is an autoimmune disease that affects oligodendrocytes
It is more common in females than in males
It is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infections
It is most often progressive in nature from onset, with gradual decline in function.
It affects both sensory and motor functions.

answer: The correct answer is D. The most common subtype of multiple sclerosis is Relapsing-Remitting MS — episodes of neurological disturbance (relapses) followed by periods of recovery (remissions). Primary progressive disease from onset is the minority pattern, so D describes the exception rather than the rule.

options.html: An abnormal sensation, typically tingling or prickling
For example, when touch is perceived as pain
Loss of sensation in the distal extremities
An inability to move a limb

answer:
The correct answer is A. The distractors are all real terms with their own names:

  • B → dysesthesia (touch perceived as pain)
  • C → could be explained by peripheral neuropathy
  • D → paralysis

weekLabel: Week 14 - Head Injury, Stroke, Headache, Seizures & Neuroinfections
lecture: Sensory symptoms & neuropathic pain
lectureMeta: Workbook Q56, Q132. Tests [[04 - Approach to Sensory Symptoms]], [[05 - Neuropathic Pain]].
stem: Which of the following symptoms is most commonly associated with neuropathic pain?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Neuropathic pain is caused by damage or dysfunction of the nervous system, resulting in abnormal pain signalling. Common characteristics: burning, shooting or stabbing pain, numbness, tingling, and sensitivity to touch or pressure. It may be intermittent or constant, and can be severe and debilitating.

It is often chronic and difficult to treat, and is associated with conditions such as diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia and spinal cord injury. Treatment: antidepressants, anticonvulsants and opioids, plus physical therapy and non-pharmacological approaches — see Q40 and Q51 for why antidepressants work.

lecture: Headache
lectureMeta: Workbook Q97-Q101. Tests [[06 - Approach to Headache]].
stem: A 21-year-old female comes to your family medical practice complaining of headaches. On history, she has had more than 10 headaches per month, but less than 15 per month, for 3 months now. The pain lasts for approximately 5 hours each time. She feels a tightening sensation bilaterally, and it is not aggravated by regular activity. She denies any nausea or vomiting, and claims she does not experience phonophobia. However, sometimes she does experience photophobia. She has tried using regular analgesics and heating pads, which sometimes relieve her pain. Which of the following types of headache does she most likely have?
answer:
The workbook's answer is A. The diagnostic criteria for episodic tension-type headache — at least 10 previous episodes fulfilling all of:

  1. Headache lasts 30 min - 7 hours
  2. Bilateral pain; a pressing/tightening sensation, NON-pulsating
  3. Mild/moderate intensity, does not prohibit activities, not aggravated by routine activity
  4. No nausea/vomiting
  5. No, or only one, of photophobia or phonophobia
  6. Usually relieved by change of position, analgesics, heat or massage

Her presentation matches every criterion, including the "only one of photo/phonophobia" clause. Tension-type headaches can be seen in patients who overuse analgesics (Q99) and may follow trauma.

flags.title: The frequency qualifier contradicts the stem
flags.html: The key's own classification states: infrequent = less than 1 day/month (under 12 days/year); frequent = more than 1 day/month but less than 15 days/month. The stem says she has more than 10 but fewer than 15 headaches per month — which makes this frequent, not infrequent, episodic tension-type headache. The headache type in A is right; the frequency label is wrong, and no option offers the frequent variant.

lecture: Headache

stem: A 40-year-old woman is referred to your neurology clinic with headaches that are preceded by a loss of vision in one eye that develops over 15 minutes. Immediately following loss of vision, she experiences a unilateral, pulsating type of headache that causes her to vomit. She is sensitive to both light and sound at this time and has to avoid even light activity such as walking, as this aggravates the headache. The headache lasts approximately 24 hours but her vision returns within an hour. She has had approximately 7 of these headaches in the last year. What type of headache is she suffering from?
answer:
The correct answer is C. An aura is a transient focal neurological symptom that can occur before a headache. The timing rules: the headache must follow the aura within 60 minutes, or occur simultaneously with / before it; and the aura must be fully reversible, develop over a few minutes, and last no longer than 1 hour — her vision returns within the hour, so it qualifies.

Migraine itself is unilateral, pulsating, aggravated by physical activity, moderate to severe enough to prevent daily activities, with either nausea/vomiting or photophobia AND phonophobia.

The key's mnemonic — SULTANS:

  • S — severe
  • UL — unilateral
  • T — throbbing
  • A — activity worsens headache
  • N — nausea/vomiting
  • S — sensitivity to light/sound

lecture: Headache
lectureMeta: Workbook Q97-Q101. Tests [[06 - Approach to Headache]].
stem: A 35-year-old female patient presents to your family medical practice complaining of headaches that are not relieved with the over the counter medications she has tried. The headache occurs almost daily, and she awakens each morning with a headache that is a different quality than the headache that she originally took the medication for. She describes this new headache as more of a dull and diffuse pain. What do you advise this patient to do?

options.html: Switch from acetaminophen to aspirin, as acetaminophen causes rebound headaches.
Prescribe her a course of sumatriptan.
Prescribe her calcium channel blockers because she is experiencing cluster headaches.
Ask her to drink coffee in the morning to relieve her headache.
Ask her to permanently discontinue the use of analgesics.

answer:
The correct answer is E. This is medication overuse headache: continued analgesic use only dulls the pain, but the headache returns requiring even more analgesic — a vicious cycle. It can also result from caffeine withdrawal during sleep, which is what makes D actively counterproductive as a strategy even though coffee would relieve the morning headache.

The only treatment is to discontinue all analgesics completely and permanently.

Prevention thresholds worth memorizing: prescribe triptans for fewer than 10 days/month and simple analgesics for fewer than 15 days/month.

lecture: Headache
lectureMeta: Workbook Q97-Q101. Tests [[06 - Approach to Headache]].
stem: A 75-year-old woman comes to see you in your family practice complaining of a severe headache most severe around her jaws and forehead, with worsening of pain when chewing food. She describes the pain as constant for 2 days now, and was not relieved with aspirin or ibuprofen. You suspect a diagnosis of __________ which is caused by __________ and the most appropriate next step is _________.

options.html: Temporal arteritis, inflammation, biopsy the temporal artery.

answer:
The correct answer is C. Temporal arteritis (giant cell arteritis) is a vasculitis caused by inflammation of the large and medium arteries of the head — not atherosclerosis, which rules out A and B. It causes headache localized around the jaw, temple or cheek, worsened with movement of the jaw (jaw claudication).

Why treatment comes before biopsy (the C-vs-E discriminator): other arteries such as the ophthalmic artery can be affected, and half of those presenting with the headache of temporal arteritis go on to develop blindness or another vascular catastrophe. So high-dose corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/day prednisone) are required as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, even before confirmatory biopsy results.

flags.title: Duplicate options
flags.html: Options A and B are verbatim identical, and so are C and D. The question as printed has only three distinct choices. C and D are equally correct; the key prints C.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to your clinic complaining of a severe, right-sided headache lasting only 30 minutes. The headache causes his eyelid to swell on the same side, and he notices only the right side of his forehead is covered in sweat during these headaches. The reason he came to see you was because they were occurring so often, about 5 times a day, every day for about a month now. What do you prescribe this patient to relieve his pain?
answer:
The correct answer is A. This is a cluster headache, which can occur from once every other day up to 8 times a day. Associated features are all ipsilateral autonomic signs: lacrimation, nasal congestion, eyelid edema, forehead and facial sweating, and miosis/ptosis — the stem gives the eyelid swelling and the unilateral forehead sweating.

Treatment of an acute attack is injected sumatriptan — note the route matters, not just the drug.

answer: The correct answer is E. The three are nested, not parallel, which is why "all of the above" rather than "both a and b": full consciousness involves cognitive awareness, which requires cerebral cortical activity; and a functional ascending RAS determines wakefulness/arousability, which is a component of alertness, which is a prerequisite for awareness.

answer: The correct answer is D — 8. Eyes 4 (spontaneous) + Verbal 1 (no response) + Motor 3 (abnormal flexion / decorticate) = 8. See the full scale at Q122, and note the mnemonic there: "GCS of 8… intubate!" See Glasgow Coma Scale.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a clinical feature of tonsillar herniation?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Tonsillar herniation results from raised intracranial pressure driving the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, affecting the lower brainstem and upper cervical cord. Its features map onto the structures compressed:

  • decreased level of consciousness ← midbrain compression
  • flaccid paralysis ← corticospinal tract compression
  • neck stiffness ← tonsillar impaction
  • respiratory irregularities ← medullary respiratory centres
  • blood pressure instability ← medullary cardiovascular centres

Upward gaze impairment belongs to central tentorial herniation, where the diencephalon is displaced through the tentorial notch and the superior colliculi are compressed.
